listeningScripts.title: Reporting Lost Property
listeningScripts.text:
Officer: Lost property, Harkness Bus Company. How can I help?
Caller: I left a bag on a bus yesterday evening.
Officer: Let's take the details. Your name first.
Caller: Tobias Kilbride. Kilbride is K-I-L-B-R-I-D-E.
Officer: And a number we can reach you on?
Caller: 07854 331 207.
Officer: Which route were you on?
Caller: The 46, towards Weatherley.
Officer: And roughly what time?
Caller: A quarter past six.
Officer: Now the bag itself. Describe it for me — and be specific, because we hold a great many black rucksacks.
Caller: It's a green canvas shoulder bag, with a leather strap.
Officer: Good, that's the kind of detail that finds things. What's in it?
Caller: A laptop, a notebook, and a set of keys.
Officer: The keys are the reason I'd like you to come in today rather than wait. Where did you sit?
Caller: Upstairs, near the back.
Officer: That's helpful too. Items from the upper deck often come in a day later than the rest, because they're found at the depot rather than by the driver.
Caller: So it might not be logged yet?
Officer: Exactly. It may be here without being on the system, so don't take a negative answer on the phone as final.
Caller: When can I come?
Officer: The counter is open until four, weekdays only, and bring photographic identification — we can't release anything without it.
Officer: One more thing. We keep items for twenty-eight days, and after that they go to a charity auction.

listeningScripts.title: Leisure Centre Induction
listeningScripts.text:
Duty manager: Good evening, and welcome to Farnley Leisure Centre. I'm Delphine, and I look after memberships.

A word about what your card actually buys, because this is where new members are most often disappointed. Membership gives you the gym, the pool and the open sessions. It does not give you classes automatically — classes are bookable, they open seven days ahead, and the popular ones fill within an hour of opening. If you want Tuesday spin, you set an alarm for the previous Tuesday morning. I would rather tell you that now than have you assume you can walk in.

Bookings are cancellable up to two hours before. Beyond that it counts as a no-show, and three no-shows in a month suspend your booking rights for a fortnight. That sounds harsh until you have watched twelve people on a waiting list for a class where four booked spaces sat empty.

The pool has lane swimming every morning until ten, and I would encourage anyone nervous about that to come anyway. The slow lane is genuinely slow, and the people in it were all new once.

Let me take you round. From this reception desk, the changing rooms are straight ahead through the double doors. The pool is beyond them on the left. The gym is upstairs, directly above reception, and the studio where classes run is at the top of the same staircase but to the right. The café overlooks the pool from the first floor, and the crèche is on the ground floor to the right of reception, next to the door you came in by.

Finally: tell the instructor about any injury before the session, not after. Every one of them would rather adapt an exercise than fill in an accident form.

listeningScripts.title: Writing Up a Null Result
listeningScripts.text:
Tutor: You look worried. What's happened with the project?
Kwabena: The experiment didn't work. I've got twelve weeks of data and no effect.
Tutor: Then you have a result. Sit down.
Kwabena: It isn't the result I proposed.
Tutor: No, and that is not the same as failure. The question is whether the study could have detected the effect if it had been there. If it could, a null result is informative. If it couldn't, the study is uninformative — and that is what we need to establish before you write anything.
Kwabena: How do I tell which?
Tutor: Start with your sample size and the size of effect you were powered to see. If you could only ever have detected something implausibly large, that is a design problem and you should say so plainly.
Kwabena: And if the design was sound?
Tutor: Then you write it up as a genuine negative finding, and you write it up confidently. Fields are distorted by exactly this — people bury null results, so the published record over-represents effects that are not really there.
Kwabena: My worry is the marker will think I did nothing.
Tutor: Markers assess the reasoning, not the outcome. I have given firsts to projects that found nothing and thirds to projects that found something by accident and could not explain how.
Kwabena: Should I try a different analysis to see if anything shows up?
Tutor: No. Testing until something turns significant is how you produce a finding that will not replicate. Report the analysis you planned. If something else looks interesting, name it as exploratory and say it needs testing on new data.
Kwabena: That feels like admitting weakness.
Tutor: It reads as competence. Anyone experienced will notice it, and it is the single clearest signal that you understood what you were doing.

listeningScripts.title: The Economics of Maintenance
listeningScripts.text:
Lecturer: Today's subject is maintenance — the least glamorous topic in infrastructure and the one that decides whether any of the rest of it works.

Begin with the asymmetry. A new bridge is opened by a politician; a repaired bridge is a lane closure that inconveniences voters. The benefits of maintenance are invisible when it succeeds, because success looks exactly like nothing happening, while the costs are immediate and highly visible. That asymmetry, not ignorance, explains most deferral. Engineers have almost always known what needed doing.

The arithmetic makes the deferral expensive. Repair costs rise sharply once deterioration passes certain thresholds — a sealed crack is cheap, a corroded reinforcement bar is not — so postponement does not spread the cost, it multiplies it. Estimates vary by structure type, but a repair delayed past the point of water ingress commonly costs several times what it would have.

There is a budgeting reason too, and it is more mundane than corruption. Capital and operating budgets are usually separate, and it is frequently easier for an authority to raise money to build something new than to fund the routine upkeep of what it already has. So systems expand faster than they are maintained, and the maintenance backlog grows even when nobody has made a decision to let it grow.

Now the part I want you to take away. The failures that make the news are rarely a surprise to the people responsible for the structure. Inspection records usually show the problem years in advance. What is missing is not information but a mechanism that converts an inspection finding into money, and the countries that have improved fastest did so by changing that mechanism — ring-fenced maintenance funds, published condition data, statutory duties to act on a rating.

So the discipline of maintenance is only partly technical. Detecting deterioration is largely solved. Being obliged to act on what you have detected is not.
